claim: The microbiota is a key determinant of the physiology and immunity of animal hosts.
source: The microbiota is a key determinant of the physiology and immunity of animal hosts.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about the role of microbiota.

claim: Bacteria serve as food for Caenorhabditis elegans and represent an integral part of the natural environment of C. elegans.
source: Bacteria serve as food for Caenorhabditis elegans and represent an integral part of the natural environment of C. elegans.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about C. elegans biology.

claim: Ochrobactrum species promoted Orsay virus transmission.
source: We observed that Ochrobactrum species promoted Orsay virus transmission, whereas Pseudomonas lurida MYb11 attenuated virus transmission relative to the standard laboratory bacterial food Escherichia coli OP50.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transmission assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pseudomonas lurida MYb11 attenuated virus transmission relative to E. coli OP50.
source: We observed that Ochrobactrum species promoted Orsay virus transmission, whereas Pseudomonas lurida MYb11 attenuated virus transmission relative to the standard laboratory bacterial food Escherichia coli OP50.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transmission assays.

claim: Pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains PA01 and PA14 further attenuated virus transmission.
source: We found that pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains PA01 and PA14 further attenuated virus transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transmission assays.

claim: The amount of Orsay virus required to infect 50% of a C. elegans population on P. lurida MYb11 compared with Ochrobactrum vermis MYb71 was dramatically increased, over three orders of magnitude.
source: We determined that the amount of Orsay virus required to infect 50% of a C. elegans population on P. lurida MYb11 compared with Ochrobactrum vermis MYb71 was dramatically increased, over three orders of magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative susceptibility assay data measuring ID50 values.

claim: Host susceptibility was attenuated even further in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: Host susceptibility was attenuated even further in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14.
evidence: This claim is supported by susceptibility assay data.

claim: Regulators of quorum sensing play a role in P. aeruginosa-mediated attenuation of C. elegans susceptibility to Orsay virus infection.
source: Genetic analysis of the determinants of P. aeruginosa required for attenuation of C. elegans susceptibility to Orsay virus infection revealed a role for regulators of quorum sensing.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis using P. aeruginosa mutants.

claim: Distinct constituents of the C. elegans microbiota and potential pathogens can have widely divergent effects on Orsay virus transmission.
source: Our data suggest that distinct constituents of the C. elegans microbiota and potential pathogens can have widely divergent effects on Orsay virus transmission, such that associated bacteria can effectively determine host susceptibility versus resistance to viral infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing different effects of different bacteria on virus transmission.

claim: Associated bacteria can effectively determine host susceptibility versus resistance to viral infection.
source: Our data suggest that distinct constituents of the C. elegans microbiota and potential pathogens can have widely divergent effects on Orsay virus transmission, such that associated bacteria can effectively determine host susceptibility versus resistance to viral infection.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing bacteria modulate host susceptibility.

claim: Tripartite host-virus-bacteria interactions play a critical role in determining the transmissibility of viruses among susceptible hosts.
source: Our study provides quantitative evidence for a critical role for tripartite host-virus-bacteria interactions in determining the transmissibility of viruses among susceptible hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data demonstrating bacteria influence virus transmission.

claim: Viruses are ubiquitous and abundant.
source: Viruses are ubiquitous and abundant (Edwards and Rohwer, 2005; Srinivasiah et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Temperature influences virus transmission.
source: Abiotic factors such as temperature (Lowen et al., 2007) and humidity (Schulman and Kilbourne, 1962) and biotic factors such as viral load (Quinn et al., 2000; Edenborough et al., 2012) and host immune status (Price et al., 2014; Chua et al., 2015) all interact to determine transmission rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Humidity influences virus transmission.
source: Abiotic factors such as temperature (Lowen et al., 2007) and humidity (Schulman and Kilbourne, 1962) and biotic factors such as viral load (Quinn et al., 2000; Edenborough et al., 2012) and host immune status (Price et al., 2014; Chua et al., 2015) all interact to determine transmission rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Viral load influences virus transmission.
source: Abiotic factors such as temperature (Lowen et al., 2007) and humidity (Schulman and Kilbourne, 1962) and biotic factors such as viral load (Quinn et al., 2000; Edenborough et al., 2012) and host immune status (Price et al., 2014; Chua et al., 2015) all interact to determine transmission rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Host immune status influences virus transmission.
source: Abiotic factors such as temperature (Lowen et al., 2007) and humidity (Schulman and Kilbourne, 1962) and biotic factors such as viral load (Quinn et al., 2000; Edenborough et al., 2012) and host immune status (Price et al., 2014; Chua et al., 2015) all interact to determine transmission rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The microbiota modulates multiple aspects of virus infection and thereby alters transmission rates among host organisms.
source: The microbiota has emerged as a host-associated factor that modulates multiple aspects of virus infection and thereby alters transmission rates among host organisms (Kane et al., 2011; Kuss et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The microbiota is critical for the proper development of the immune system.
source: In general, the microbiota is critical for the proper development of the immune system and for the effective activation of antimicrobial immune responses even at sites distal to microbiota colonization (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The microbiota is critical for the effective activation of antimicrobial immune responses even at sites distal to microbiota colonization.
source: In general, the microbiota is critical for the proper development of the immune system and for the effective activation of antimicrobial immune responses even at sites distal to microbiota colonization (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Bacteria and bacterial surface structures such as lipopolysaccharide and peptidoglycan stabilize poliovirus and reovirus in vitro.
source: More specifically, bacteria and bacterial surface structures such as lipopolysaccharide and peptidoglycan have been shown to stabilize poliovirus and reovirus in vitro (Kuss et al., 2011; Berger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microbiota depletion by antibiotic treatment was sufficient to provide protection against poliovirus and reovirus in mice.
source: These observations likely explain why microbiota depletion by antibiotic treatment was sufficient to provide protection against the same viruses in mice (Kuss et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The bacterial symbiont Wolbachia protects numerous insect species from multiple viruses either by upregulating antiviral defenses or competing for intracellular nutrients.
source: The bacterial symbiont Wolbachia protects numerous insect species from multiple viruses either by upregulating antiviral defenses or competing for intracellular nutrients (Hedges et al., 1979; Teixeira et al., 2008; Moreira et al., 2009; Bian et al., 2010; Pimentel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Serratia marcescens promoted infection of the mosquito Aedes aegypti by Dengue, Zika, and Sindbis viruses by secreting a protein, enhancin, that degrades the mucus layer covering epithelial cells.
source: Individual bacteria have also been found to enhance viral infection; Serratia marcescens promoted infection of the mosquito Aedes aegypti by Dengue, Zika, and Sindbis viruses by secreting a protein, enhancin, that degrades the mucus layer covering epithelial cells (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans is a nematode often found in microbially rich environments such as rotting vegetation.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans is a nematode often found in microbially rich environments such as rotting vegetation (Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The first naturally occurring virus capable of infecting C. elegans was isolated from Orsay, France.
source: The first naturally occurring virus capable of infecting the C. elegans was isolated from Orsay, France (Félix et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Orsay virus is a part of a group of nematode infecting viruses closely related to the Nodaviridae family of viruses which infect arthropods and fish.
source: Orsay virus is a part of a group of nematode infecting viruses closely related to the Nodaviridae family of viruses which infect arthropods and fish (Félix et al., 2011; Félix and Wang, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Orsay virus is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus with a bipartite genome.
source: Like other Nodaviruses, Orsay virus is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus with a bipartite genome (Félix et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Transmission of Orsay virus occurs horizontally through the fecal-oral route.
source: Transmission of Orsay virus occurs horizontally through the fecal-oral route.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about Orsay virus.

claim: Orsay virus solely infects C. elegans intestinal cells.
source: Fluorescence in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence imaging has revealed that Orsay virus solely infects C. elegans intestinal cells (Félix et al., 2011; Franz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Viral infection activates host defense mechanisms including the RNA-interference response and a transcriptional program known as the intracellular pathogen response.
source: Viral infection activates host defense mechanisms including the RNA-interference response and a transcriptional program known as the intracellular pathogen response (Félix et al., 2011; Sarkies et al., 2013; Bakowski et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Le Pen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C. elegans is a bacterivore and is propagated in the laboratory on lawns of Escherichia coli OP50.
source: C. elegans is a bacterivore and is propagated in the laboratory on lawns of Escherichia coli OP50.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about C. elegans laboratory culture.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen of humans found in the soil and water and can also infect C. elegans.
source: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an opportunistic pathogen of humans, is found in the soil and water and can also infect C. elegans (Tan et al., 1999a; Crone et al., 2020; Pelegrin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Infection of C. elegans with P. aeruginosa activates innate immunity and stress responses, as well as behavioral avoidance responses.
source: Infection of C. elegans with P. aeruginosa activates innate immunity and stress responses, as well as behavioral avoidance responses (Kim et al., 2002; Kim and Ewbank, 2018; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The intestinal lumen of free-dwelling C. elegans is occupied by taxonomically and functionally diverse bacteria that can affect C. elegans fitness and physiology.
source: The intestinal lumen of free-dwelling C. elegans is occupied by taxonomically and functionally diverse bacteria that can affect C. elegans fitness and physiology (Dirksen et al., 2016; Samuel et al., 2016; Dirksen, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Orsay virus spreads horizontally through the fecal-oral route and transmission can spread from a single animal to a population of animals on a plate.
source: Orsay virus spreads horizontally through the fecal-oral route and transmission can spread from a single animal to a population of animals on a plate (Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: All animals were raised to young adulthood on lawns of E. coli OP50 to eliminate differences in developmental rates caused by different bacteria.
source: All animals were raised to young adulthood on lawns of E. coli OP50 to eliminate differences in developmental rates caused by different bacteria (Dirksen, 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation explaining the rationale.

claim: The pals-5p::GFP reporter is induced by infection with Orsay virus.
source: We quantified the incidence proportion, defined as the number of new infections produced after 24 hr as determined by detection of induction of the pals-5p::GFP reporter, which is induced by infection with Orsay virus (Figure 1A–C; Bakowski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Two Ochrobactrum species increased the incidence proportion 2.7-fold and 2.9-fold compared to E. coli OP50.
source: Two Ochrobactrum species promoted virus infection in nearly all individuals in the transmission assay and increased the incidence proportion 2.7-fold and 2.9-fold compared to E. coli OP50 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Transmission from the initial spreader animals in the assay, and not multiple rounds of infection, was responsible for the increased incidence proportion observed in the presence of Ochrobactrum vermis MYb71.
source: We confirmed that transmission from the initial spreader animals in the assay, and not multiple rounds of infection, was responsible for the increased incidence proportion observed in the presence of Ochrobactrum vermis MYb71 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of Pseudomonas lurida MYb11 reduced the incidence proportion 4.1-fold compared to E. coli OP50 and 11-fold compared to O. vermis MYb71.
source: On the other hand, the presence of Pseudomonas lurida MYb11 reduced the incidence proportion 4.1-fold compared to E. coli OP50 and 11-fold compared to O. vermis MYb71 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: On average, 3.6 μL of Orsay virus stock was required to infect 50% of a population of ZD2611 animals in the presence of E. coli OP50 after 24 hr.
source: On average, 3.6 μL of Orsay virus stock prepared as indicated in the Materials and methods was required to infect 50% of a population of ZD2611 animals in the presence of E. coli OP50 after 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ID50 in the presence of E. coli OP50 was 14-fold higher than the ID50 in the presence of O. vermis MYb71.
source: We further quantified the ID50 in the presence of each bacterium and on average we observed that the ID50 in the presence of E. coli OP50 was 14-fold higher than the ID50 in the presence of O. vermis MYb71 (Figure 1D and E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ID50 observed in the presence of P. lurida was 120-fold and 1800-fold higher than the ID50 in the presence of E. coli OP50 or O. vermis MYb71, respectively.
source: The ID50 observed in the presence of P. lurida was 120-fold and 1800-fold higher than the ID50 in the presence of E. coli OP50 or O. vermis MYb71, respectively (Figure 1D and E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: At lower doses the presence of O. vermis MYb71 resulted in a greater fraction of infected animals compared to E. coli OP50 or P. lurida MYb11.
source: As expected, we observed that at lower doses the presence of O. vermis MYb71 resulted in a greater fraction of infected animals compared to E. coli OP50 or P. lurida MYb11, while at higher doses the presence of P. lurida MYb11 resulted in a reduced fraction of infected animals (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At higher doses the presence of P. lurida MYb11 resulted in a reduced fraction of infected animals.
source: As expected, we observed that at lower doses the presence of O. vermis MYb71 resulted in a greater fraction of infected animals compared to E. coli OP50 or P. lurida MYb11, while at higher doses the presence of P. lurida MYb11 resulted in a reduced fraction of infected animals (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Individual members of the C. elegans microbiota can modulate host susceptibility to Orsay virus over three orders of magnitude.
source: Together these data establish that individual members of the C. elegans microbiota can modulate host susceptibility to Orsay virus over three orders of magnitude with dramatic consequences for the transmissibility of Orsay virus.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data on ID50 values.

claim: After 6 hr of exposure to E. coli OP50, P. lurida MYb11, or O. vermis MYb71, there were no differences in pharyngeal pumping rates.
source: After 6 hr of exposure to E. coli OP50, P. lurida MYb11, or O. vermis MYb71, there were no differences in pharyngeal pumping rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: At 24 hr pumping rates were decreased in the presence of O. vermis MYb71 to an average of 242 ppm compared to 261 ppm in the presence of P. lurida MYb11.
source: At 24 hr pumping rates were decreased in the presence of O. vermis MYb71 to an average of 242 ppm compared to 261 ppm in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 suggesting that changes to feeding behavior are unlikely to be responsible for observed effects on host susceptibility to Orsay virus (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Changes to feeding behavior are unlikely to be responsible for observed effects on host susceptibility to Orsay virus.
source: At 24 hr pumping rates were decreased in the presence of O. vermis MYb71 to an average of 242 ppm compared to 261 ppm in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 suggesting that changes to feeding behavior are unlikely to be responsible for observed effects on host susceptibility to Orsay virus (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pharyngeal pumping data.

claim: In the presence of P. aeruginosa strains PA01 or PA14, transmission from spreader animals to uninfected individuals was nearly completely blocked.
source: We observed that in the presence of either P. aeruginosa strains PA01 or PA14, transmission from spreader animals to uninfected individuals was nearly completely blocked and the incidence proportion was 11-fold and 32-fold lower than that observed in the presence of E. coli OP50, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The incidence proportion in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA01 and PA14 was 11-fold and 32-fold lower than that observed in the presence of E. coli OP50, respectively.
source: We observed that in the presence of either P. aeruginosa strains PA01 or PA14, transmission from spreader animals to uninfected individuals was nearly completely blocked and the incidence proportion was 11-fold and 32-fold lower than that observed in the presence of E. coli OP50, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The attenuating effect of P. aeruginosa PA01 and PA14 on virus transmission was further reduced 3.1-fold and 9.5-fold, respectively, compared to the incidence proportion observed in the presence of P. lurida MYb11.
source: The attenuating effect of P. aeruginosa PA01 and PA14 on virus transmission was further reduced 3.1-fold and 9.5-fold, respectively, compared to the incidence proportion observed in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At the highest dose of virus used, 0.5% of the animals were infected in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 as compared to 54%, 70%, and 97% in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA01, P. lurida MYb11, or E. coli OP50, respectively.
source: At the highest dose of virus used, we still observed robust attenuation of infection in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 as 0.5% of the animals were infected as compared to 54%, 70%, and 97% in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA01, P. lurida MYb11, or E. coli OP50, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No individuals were detectably infected with Orsay virus while in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 using FISH staining.
source: We confirmed that no individuals were detectably infected with Orsay virus while in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 using FISH staining (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The presence of P. aeruginosa PA01 and P. lurida MYb11 attenuated average infection to 24% and 60% of the population respectively compared to E. coli OP50 which supported infection of 86% of the population.
source: FISH additionally confirmed that the presence of P. aeruginosa PA01 and P. lurida MYb11 attenuated average infection to 24% and 60% of the population respectively compared to E. coli OP50 which supported infection of 86% of the population.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data.

claim: P. aeruginosa PA01, P. lurida MYb11, and E. coli OP50 all supported higher levels of infection than P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: Further, P. aeruginosa PA01, P. lurida MYb11, and E. coli OP50 all supported higher levels of infection than P. aeruginosa PA14 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There were no differences observed in pharyngeal pumping rate after 6 hr of exposure to each bacterium.
source: There were no differences observed in pharyngeal pumping rate after 6 hr of exposure to each bacterium (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: After 24 hr pharyngeal pumping rate increased in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 to an average of 264 ppm compared to 248 ppm in the presence of E. coli OP50.
source: After 24 hr pharyngeal pumping rate increased in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 to an average of 264 ppm compared to 248 ppm in the presence of E. coli OP50 which suggests that changes to feeding behavior are unlikely to account for the attenuation of infection observed in P. aeruginosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Changes to feeding behavior are unlikely to account for the attenuation of infection observed in P. aeruginosa.
source: After 24 hr pharyngeal pumping rate increased in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 to an average of 264 ppm compared to 248 ppm in the presence of E. coli OP50 which suggests that changes to feeding behavior are unlikely to account for the attenuation of infection observed in P. aeruginosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pharyngeal pumping data.

claim: P. aeruginosa is a pathogen of C. elegans and numerous other organisms.
source: P. aeruginosa is a pathogen of C. elegans and numerous other organisms (Tan et al., 1999a; Rahme et al., 1995; Tan et al., 1999b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PA14 is more virulent toward C. elegans than PA01.
source: Moreover, while both PA01 and PA14 are pathogenic, PA14 is more virulent toward C. elegans (Tan et al., 1999a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P. lurida MYb11 promotes developmental rate and fitness, although does so at a minor cost to overall lifespan.
source: P. lurida MYb11 promotes developmental rate and fitness, although does so at a minor cost to overall lifespan (Dirksen, 2020; Kissoyan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Under the assay conditions, substantial mortality is not observed until 72 hr after exposure.
source: Under our assay conditions, including a full lawn of bacteria, which prevent C. elegans from avoiding undesirable bacteria, and a temperature of 20°C, which is below the optimal virulence temperature of P. aeruginosa, substantial mortality is not observed until 72 hr after exposure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All bacteria enhanced mortality in comparison to E. coli OP50.
source: All bacteria enhanced mortality in comparison to E. coli OP50 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: O. vermis MYb71 exposure led to similarly enhanced mortality when compared to P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: Interestingly, O. vermis MYb71 exposure led to similarly enhanced mortality when compared to P. aeruginosa PA14, and both bacteria enhanced mortality in comparison to P. lurida MYb11 or P. aeruginosa PA01 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: P. lurida MYb11 enhanced mortality compared to P. aeruginosa PA01 under these conditions.
source: P. lurida MYb11 also enhanced mortality compared to P. aeruginosa PA01 under these conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The similar lifespans of animals exposed to P. aeruginosa PA14 and O. vermis MYb71 stand in contrast to their divergent effects on host susceptibility to Orsay virus.
source: The similar lifespans of animals exposed to P. aeruginosa PA14 and O. vermis MYb71 stand in contrast to their divergent effects on host susceptibility to Orsay virus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing lifespan and susceptibility data.

claim: General pathogenicity is unlikely to be responsible for effects on host susceptibility.
source: This suggests that general pathogenicity is unlikely to be responsible for effects on host susceptibility, although pathogenic consequences specific to exposure to each bacterium may still contribute to the observed effects on host susceptibility to Orsay virus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lifespan and susceptibility data.

claim: Orsay virus RNA1 replication efficiency was unaffected by the presence of Pseudomonas species relative to RNA1 replication observed in the presence of E. coli OP50.
source: Using this system, we observed that Orsay virus RNA1 replication efficiency was unaffected by the presence of Pseudomonas species relative to RNA1 replication observed in the presence of E. coli OP50 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using a plasmid-based replication system shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There were no differences observed in heat-shock efficiency between the different bacteria.
source: Additionally, there were no differences observed in heat-shock efficiency between the different bacteria (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Bacteria-induced differences in RNA1 replication in the host do not explain the substantial attenuation of Orsay virus transmission and infection rates caused by P. aeruginosa PA01 or PA14 and P. lurida MYb11.
source: These data suggest that bacteria-induced differences in RNA1 replication in the host do not explain the substantial attenuation of Orsay virus transmission and infection rates caused by P. aeruginosa PA01 or PA14 and P. lurida MYb11.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the plasmid-based replication data.

claim: In rde-1(ne219) animals viral RNA1 levels increased at 24 hr relative to 2 hr post exposure regardless of the bacteria present.
source: In rde-1(ne219) animals viral RNA1 levels increased at 24 hr relative to 2 hr post exposure regardless of the bacteria present (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: In the wild-type background replication was not observed in animals exposed to P. aeruginosa PA14 and was attenuated in animals exposed to P. aeruginosa PA01 compared to animals exposed to E. coli OP50 or P. lurida MYb11.
source: On the other hand, in the wild-type background replication was not observed in animals exposed to P. aeruginosa PA14 and was attenuated in animals exposed to P. aeruginosa PA01 compared to animals exposed to E. coli OP50 or P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The viral load observed in the wild-type populations is likely due to a smaller proportion of the population being infected, rather than hampered replication.
source: It is therefore likely that the viral load we observed in the wild-type populations is due to a smaller proportion of the population being infected, rather than hampered replication (Félix et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the qPCR data and cited literature.

claim: Orsay virus is not rapidly degraded in the presence of P. lurida MYb11, P. aeruginosa PA01, or P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: We did not observe a substantial decrease in viral stability in the presence of any bacterium suggesting Orsay virus is not rapidly degraded (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral stability assay data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: An approximately twofold decrease in viral levels between E. coli OP50 and P. lurida MYb11 already existed within 30 min of exposure to each bacterium and did not grow further over the course of 24 hr.
source: We did observe an approximately twofold decrease in viral levels between E. coli OP50 and P. lurida MYb11, however, this difference already existed within 30 min of exposure to each bacterium and did not grow further over the course of 24 hr suggesting we are measuring differences in recovery of Orsay virus from each bacterial lawn, rather than enhanced degradation in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral stability assay data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Differences in viral levels between E. coli OP50 and P. lurida MYb11 reflect differences in recovery of Orsay virus from each bacterial lawn, rather than enhanced degradation in the presence of P. lurida MYb11.
source: We did observe an approximately twofold decrease in viral levels between E. coli OP50 and P. lurida MYb11, however, this difference already existed within 30 min of exposure to each bacterium and did not grow further over the course of 24 hr suggesting we are measuring differences in recovery of Orsay virus from each bacterial lawn, rather than enhanced degradation in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the viral stability data.

claim: There was no substantial decrease in viral shedding in the presence of any bacterium.
source: We did not observe a substantial decrease in viral shedding in the presence of any bacterium (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral shedding assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Approximately fourfold lower levels of Orsay virus were shed in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 vs E. coli OP50.
source: We observed approximately fourfold lower levels of Orsay virus shed in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 vs E. coli OP50, but as suggested by our virus stability data, we believe these differences at least partly reflect differences in Orsay virus recovery from each bacterial lawn rather than actual differences in viral shedding (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral shedding assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Differences in Orsay virus levels shed in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 vs E. coli OP50 at least partly reflect differences in Orsay virus recovery from each bacterial lawn rather than actual differences in viral shedding.
source: We observed approximately fourfold lower levels of Orsay virus shed in the presence of P. lurida MYb11 vs E. coli OP50, but as suggested by our virus stability data, we believe these differences at least partly reflect differences in Orsay virus recovery from each bacterial lawn rather than actual differences in viral shedding (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the viral shedding and stability data.

claim: P. aeruginosa relies upon three quorum sensing systems: las, rhl, and pqs.
source: P. aeruginosa relies upon three quorum sensing systems: las, rhl, and pqs.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about P. aeruginosa quorum sensing.

claim: The quorum sensing systems in P. aeruginosa are arranged hierarchically, however crosstalk between them is extensive.
source: These systems are arranged hierarchically, however crosstalk between them is extensive (Figure 4A; Lee and Zhang, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The gacA/gacS two-component regulatory system regulates numerous genes that together influence quorum sensing, virulence, and biofilm development.
source: In P. aeruginosa, an additional layer of regulation stems from two-component regulatory systems such as gacA/gacS which regulates numerous genes that together influence quorum sensing, virulence, and biofilm development (Figure 4A; Reimmann et al., 1997; Parkins et al., 2001; Brencic et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: P. aeruginosa PA01 preferentially produces Psl while P. aeruginosa PA14 is unable to synthesize Psl and produce Pel.
source: However, P. aeruginosa PA01 preferentially produces Psl while P. aeruginosa PA14 is unable to synthesize Psl and produce Pel (Friedman and Kolter, 2004a; Friedman and Kolter, 2004b; Franklin et al., 2011; Jackson et al., 2004; Matsukawa and Greenberg, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutations of any the regulators of the las, rhl, or pqs quorum sensing systems suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection caused by the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA01.
source: Mutations of any the regulators of the las, rhl, or pqs quorum sensing systems suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection caused by the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA01 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockout of gacA in P. aeruginosa PA01 suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection.
source: Knockout of gacA in P. aeruginosa PA01 also suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutation of any of the three exopolysaccharide production pathways had no potent effect on the attenuation of infection.
source: On the other hand, mutation of any of the three exopolysaccharide production pathways had no potent effect on the attenuation of infection (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Quorum sensing regulated processes play a role in reducing Orsay virus infection rates.
source: These data support a role for quorum sensing regulated processes in reducing Orsay virus infection rates but do not implicate a role for individual exopolysaccharides.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis data.

claim: Individual exopolysaccharides do not play a role in reducing Orsay virus infection rates.
source: These data support a role for quorum sensing regulated processes in reducing Orsay virus infection rates but do not implicate a role for individual exopolysaccharides.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis data.

claim: Mutation of gacA or rhlR in P. aeruginosa PA14 suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection observed in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: For P. aeruginosa PA14, mutation of gacA or rhlR suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection observed in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of the rhlR regulators rhlI or pqsE alone had no effect on the attenuation of Orsay virus infection.
source: Loss of the rhlR regulators rhlI or pqsE alone had no effect on the attenuation of Orsay virus infection, but simultaneous mutation of both rhlI and pqsE did suppress the attenuation of Orsay virus infection observed in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14, similar to that observed for the rhlR mutant, suggesting rhlI and pqsE function redundantly to regulate rhlR in this context (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Mukherjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Simultaneous mutation of both rhlI and pqsE suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection observed in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: Loss of the rhlR regulators rhlI or pqsE alone had no effect on the attenuation of Orsay virus infection, but simultaneous mutation of both rhlI and pqsE did suppress the attenuation of Orsay virus infection observed in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14, similar to that observed for the rhlR mutant, suggesting rhlI and pqsE function redundantly to regulate rhlR in this context (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Mukherjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: rhlI and pqsE function redundantly to regulate rhlR in this context.
source: Loss of the rhlR regulators rhlI or pqsE alone had no effect on the attenuation of Orsay virus infection, but simultaneous mutation of both rhlI and pqsE did suppress the attenuation of Orsay virus infection observed in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14, similar to that observed for the rhlR mutant, suggesting rhlI and pqsE function redundantly to regulate rhlR in this context (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Mukherjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis data and supported by citation.

claim: Mutation of lasI or lasR suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection to a lesser extent.
source: Mutation of lasI or lasR suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection to a lesser extent (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Independent mutation of two genes responsible for pel or alg exopolysaccharide production had no effect on infection rates.
source: Independent mutation of two genes responsible for pel or alg exopolysaccharide production had no effect on infection rates (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of rhlR and gacA in P. aeruginosa PA01 or P. aeruginosa PA14 suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection.
source: We further confirmed that mutation of rhlR and gacA in P. aeruginosa PA01 or P. aeruginosa PA14 suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus infection via FISH (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Quorum sensing plays a role in mediating P. aeruginosa PA14 suppression of Orsay virus infection.
source: These data suggest a role for quorum sensing in mediating P. aeruginosa PA14 suppression of Orsay virus infection, as we observed for P. aeruginosa PA01.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis data.

claim: There may be some differential regulation of the bacterial effectors responsible in P. aeruginosa PA14 compared to P. aeruginosa PA01, or additional non-quorum sensing-related factors that also mediate suppression.
source: However, our results obtained in the presence of P. aeruginosa PA14 suggest that there may be some differential regulation of the bacterial effectors responsible in comparison to P. aeruginosa PA01, or additional non-quorum sensing-related factors that also mediate suppression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences between PA01 and PA14 mutant effects.

claim: All P. aeruginosa PA01 quorum sensing mutants suppressed the attenuation of transmission by increasing the incidence proportion >6-fold compared to the wild-type P. aeruginosa PA01.
source: All P. aeruginosa PA01 quorum sensing mutants suppressed the attenuation of transmission by increasing the incidence proportion >6-fold compared to the wild-type P. aeruginosa PA01 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: P. aeruginosa PA14 rhlR and gacA mutants suppressed the attenuation of transmission by increasing the incidence proportion 19-fold and 17-fold respectively compared to wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: P. aeruginosa PA14 rhlR and gacA mutants suppressed the attenuation of transmission by increasing the incidence proportion 19-fold and 17-fold respectively compared to wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14, but a lasI mutant had minimal effect consistent with the pattern we observed in the susceptibility assay using exogenous Orsay virus (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A P. aeruginosa PA14 lasI mutant had minimal effect on transmission consistent with the pattern observed in the susceptibility assay using exogenous Orsay virus.
source: P. aeruginosa PA14 rhlR and gacA mutants suppressed the attenuation of transmission by increasing the incidence proportion 19-fold and 17-fold respectively compared to wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14, but a lasI mutant had minimal effect consistent with the pattern we observed in the susceptibility assay using exogenous Orsay virus (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The magnitude of suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus transmission observed in the P. aeruginosa rhlR or gacA mutants was greater in the P. aeruginosa PA01 background compared to the P. aeruginosa PA14 background.
source: Likewise, the magnitude of suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus transmission observed in the P. aeruginosa rhlR or gacA mutants was greater in the P. aeruginosa PA01 background compared to the P. aeruginosa PA14 background, potentially suggesting the existence of additional strain specific factors that act in P. aeruginosa PA14 to attenuate Orsay virus transmission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transmission assay data.

claim: There may be additional strain specific factors that act in P. aeruginosa PA14 to attenuate Orsay virus transmission.
source: Likewise, the magnitude of suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus transmission observed in the P. aeruginosa rhlR or gacA mutants was greater in the P. aeruginosa PA01 background compared to the P. aeruginosa PA14 background, potentially suggesting the existence of additional strain specific factors that act in P. aeruginosa PA14 to attenuate Orsay virus transmission.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences between PA01 and PA14.

claim: No potent effect on host susceptibility to infection by Orsay virus was observed from any bacterial culture supernatant.
source: We did not observe any potent effect on host susceptibility to infection by Orsay virus from any supernatant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), although it is difficult to rule out the possibility that the compounds may act at concentrations that are locally higher than the concentrations at which the compounds are present in our experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: It is difficult to rule out the possibility that quorum sensing compounds may act at concentrations that are locally higher than the concentrations at which the compounds are present in the supernatant experiments.
source: We did not observe any potent effect on host susceptibility to infection by Orsay virus from any supernatant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), although it is difficult to rule out the possibility that the compounds may act at concentrations that are locally higher than the concentrations at which the compounds are present in our experiments.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of the supernatant experiments.

claim: 18 putative hits, including lasI, rhlR, and gacA, were identified from the candidate-based screen with the corresponding P. aeruginosa PA14 mutants exhibiting suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus infection by wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: Of the 211 genes tested, 18 putative hits, including lasI, rhlR, and gacA, were identified with the corresponding P. aeruginosa PA14 mutants exhibiting suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus infection by wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14 (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Six of the 15 novel candidate genes were confirmed as hits in additional susceptibility assays.
source: Using the 15 novel candidate genes, we performed an additional set of susceptibility assays which confirmed six of the hits (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transposon insertion in the genes ptsP, prpC, and kinB led to marked suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus leading to infection of 97%, 89%, and 82% of the population respectively compared to infection in only 4.2% of the population in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: Transposon insertion in the genes ptsP, prpC, and kinB led to marked suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus leading to infection of 97%, 89%, and 82% of the population respectively compared to infection in only 4.2% of the population in the presence of wild-type P. aeruginosa PA14 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transposon insertion in three additional genes, clpA, glnK, and fabF1, resulted in weaker, but robust suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus leading to infection of 34%, 28%, and 17% of the population respectively.
source: Transposon insertion in three additional genes, clpA, glnK, and fabF1, resulted in weaker, but robust suppression of the attenuation of Orsay virus leading to infection of 34%, 28%, and 17% of the population respectively (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only mutation of ptsP led to statistically significant suppression of Orsay virus attenuation in the transmission assay.
source: While we observed a trend toward mutations affecting susceptibility also affecting virus transmission, we observed a high degree of variation in the transmission assay, such that only mutation of ptsP led to statistically significant suppression of Orsay virus attenuation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All six confirmed hits originated from the set of genes required for full P. aeruginosa PA14 virulence in C. elegans.
source: We noted that all six of the hits originated from the set of genes required for full P. aeruginosa PA14 virulence in C. elegans (Feinbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the screen results supported by citation.

claim: The six hits represented only 6 out of the 41 tested genes that are known to influence virulence, indicative of some degree of specificity in the consequences of these mutations beyond their general effect on P. aeruginosa PA14 virulence.
source: These hits represented only 6 out of the 41 tested genes that are known to influence virulence, indicative of some degree of specificity in the consequences of these mutations beyond their general effect on P. aeruginosa PA14 virulence (Feinbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the screen results.

claim: Knockout of gacA in P. lurida MYb11 led to infection of 77% of the population compared to infection of 43% of the population in the presence of wild-type P. lurida MYb11 from exogenous Orsay virus.
source: Following exposure to exogenous Orsay virus, knockout of gacA in P. lurida MYb11 led to infection of 77% of the population compared to infection of 43% of the population in the presence of wild-type P. lurida MYb11 from exogenous Orsay virus (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gacA mutant of P. lurida MYb11 supported infection of 62% of the population versus 37% infection in the presence of wild-type P. lurida MYb11 as confirmed via FISH.
source: These observations were confirmed via FISH, as the gacA mutant supported infection of 62% of the population versus 37% infection in the presence of wild-type P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The gacA mutation in P. lurida MYb11 suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus transmission, increasing the incidence proportion 2.9-fold compared to wild-type P. lurida MYb11.
source: The gacA mutation also suppressed the attenuation of Orsay virus transmission, increasing the incidence proportion 2.9-fold compared to wild-type P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: gacA has a conserved role between P. aeruginosa and P. lurida MYb11 in the attenuation of Orsay virus transmission and infection of C. elegans.
source: These data suggest that gacA has a conserved role between P. aeruginosa and P. lurida MYb11 in the attenuation of Orsay virus transmission and infection of C. elegans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis data in both species.

claim: Knockout of the P. lurida MYb11 orthologs of ptsP, prpC, or kinB failed to suppress the attenuation of Orsay virus infection or transmission by P. lurida MYb11.
source: On the other hand, knockout of the P. lurida MYb11 orthologs of ptsP, prpC, or kinB failed to suppress the attenuation of Orsay virus infection or transmission by P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 6E,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D; Feinbaum et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E, F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: ptsP, prpC, and kinB may play different roles within P. lurida MYb11 and P. aeruginosa and therefore their mutation did not have the same consequences for Orsay virus attenuation.
source: One explanation of these results is that these genes play different roles within P. lurida MYb11 and P. aeruginosa and therefore their mutation did not have the same consequences for Orsay virus attenuation.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the genetic analysis results.

claim: ptsP, prpC, and kinB may act to attenuate Orsay virus infection via some specific effect on P. aeruginosa PA14 virulence but do not influence the interaction of P. lurida MYb11 with C. elegans.
source: Alternatively, these results might suggest that ptsP, prpC, and kinB act to attenuate Orsay virus infection via some specific effect on P. aeruginosa PA14 virulence but do not influence the interaction of P. lurida MYb11 with C. elegans.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the genetic analysis results.

claim: A 50% mixture of O. vermis MYb71 and P. lurida MYb11 attenuated infection to the same degree as pure P. lurida MYb11.
source: When cultures of O. vermis MYb71 and P. lurida MYb11 were concentrated to 25 mg/mL and then mixed, we observed that a 50% mixture of each bacterium (vol:vol) attenuated infection to the same degree as pure P. lurida MYb11 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mixing O. vermis MYb71 with E. coli OP50 lead to infection rates similar to pure E. coli OP50.
source: Moreover, we also noted that mixing O. vermis MYb71 with E. coli OP50 also lead to infection rates similar to pure E. coli OP50 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Ochrobactrum is found in large numbers in the C. elegans intestine following exposure.
source: Previous studies have identified that Ochrobactrum is found in large numbers in the C. elegans intestine following exposure (Dirksen et al., 2016; Dirksen, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GFP expressing Ochrobactrum BH3 was readily observed within the intestine at 4 hr or 24 hr of exposure when alone.
source: When alone, GFP expressing Ochrobactrum BH3 was readily observed within the intestine at 4 hr or 24 hr of exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Exposure to a mixed lawn of Ochrobactrum BH3 and P. lurida MYb11 reduced intestinal accumulation of Ochrobactrum BH3 compared to the pure Ochrobactrum BH3 treatment.
source: Interestingly, exposure to a mixed lawn of Ochrobactrum BH3 and P. lurida MYb11 reduced intestinal accumulation of Ochrobactrum BH3 compared to the pure Ochrobactrum BH3 treatment (Figure 7B and C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B, C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Exposure to a mixed lawn of Ochrobactrum BH3 and E. coli OP50 reduced accumulation of Ochrobactrum BH3 at 4 hr compared to a pure Ochrobactrum BH3 treatment, but this difference was minimal by 24 hr.
source: On the other hand, exposure to a mixed lawn of Ochrobactrum BH3 and E. coli OP50 reduced accumulation of Ochrobactrum BH3 at 4 hr compared to a pure Ochrobactrum BH3 treatment, but this difference was minimal by 24 hr (Figure 7B and C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B, C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: O. vermis MYb71 was readily observed in the intestinal lumen at 4 hr or 24 hr of exposure.
source: As expected from our fluorescence experiments, O. vermis MYb71 was readily observed in the intestinal lumen at 4 hr or 24 hr of exposure (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The glycocalyx is the mucus-like layer covering C. elegans intestinal cells.
source: The glycocalyx is the mucus-like layer covering C. elegans intestinal cells and that recent work has suggested may play a role in defense against Orsay virus (McGhee, 2007; Zhou et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recent work has suggested the glycocalyx may play a role in defense against Orsay virus.
source: The glycocalyx is the mucus-like layer covering C. elegans intestinal cells and that recent work has suggested may play a role in defense against Orsay virus (McGhee, 2007; Zhou et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The glycocalyx of animals exposed to O. vermis MYb71 was observed with regions of variable thickness and potential instances of O. vermis MYb71 deforming the microvilli brush border.
source: The glycocalyx of animals exposed to O. vermis MYb71 was observed with regions of variable thickness and potential instances of O. vermis MYb71 deforming the microvilli brush border as opposed to animals exposed to E. coli OP50 where the glycocalyx appeared uniform and undisturbed (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The glycocalyx of animals exposed to E. coli OP50 appeared uniform and undisturbed.
source: The glycocalyx of animals exposed to O. vermis MYb71 was observed with regions of variable thickness and potential instances of O. vermis MYb71 deforming the microvilli brush border as opposed to animals exposed to E. coli OP50 where the glycocalyx appeared uniform and undisturbed (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: O. vermis MYb71 mediated disruption of the brush border and glycocalyx may promote Orsay virus infection.
source: These observations lead us to speculate that O. vermis MYb71 mediated disruption of the brush border and glycocalyx promotes Orsay virus infection although this hypothesis has yet to be tested.
evidence: This is speculation based on the electron microscopy observations and comparison to S. marcescens.

claim: Host susceptibility to Orsay virus infection may vary by over three orders of magnitude in the presence of O. vermis MYb71 versus P. lurida MYb11.
source: Our results using exogenous virus demonstrate that host susceptibility to Orsay virus infection may vary by over three orders of magnitude in the presence of O. vermis MYb71 versus P. lurida MYb11 which are found in the natural environment in association with C. elegans (Dirksen et al., 2016; Dirksen, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ID50 data and citations about bacterial natural occurrence.

claim: Pathogenic P. aeruginosa, which may be found in natural environments, can further attenuate Orsay virus transmission.
source: Moreover, we observe that pathogenic P. aeruginosa, which may be found in natural environments, can further attenuate Orsay virus transmission (Crone et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citation about P. aeruginosa in natural environments.

claim: The work is consistent with a recent study by González and Félix that also reported that monoaxenic cultures of other bacteria from the environment of C. elegans impact host susceptibility.
source: Our work is also consistent with a recent study by González and Félix that also reported that monoaxenic cultures of other bacteria from the environment of C. elegans impact host susceptibility (González and Félix, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Ochrobactrum intermedium promoted poliovirus infection in mice and enhanced poliovirus stability in vitro.
source: Ochrobactrum intermedium promoted poliovirus infection in mice and enhanced poliovirus stability in vitro (Kuss et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ochrobactrum anthropi was identified using a random forest analysis as one of the most predictive features differentiating the upper respiratory tract of human patients recovering from influenza infection versus healthy controls.
source: Ochrobactrum anthropi, an opportunistic human pathogen, was identified using a random forest analysis as one of the most predictive features differentiating the upper respiratory tract of human patients recovering from influenza infection versus healthy controls (Kaul et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ochrobactrum colonization may have roles in evolutionarily diverse hosts in modulating viral infection.
source: Our observations in the C. elegans host raise the speculative possibility that Ochrobactrum colonization may have roles in evolutionarily diverse hosts in modulating viral infection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observations in C. elegans and previous literature.

claim: Individual bacteria can have a profound impact on Orsay virus transmission rates in a species-specific manner.
source: Our data demonstrate that individual bacteria can have a profound impact on Orsay virus transmission rates in a species-specific manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing different effects of different bacteria.

claim: The tractability of the C. elegans-Orsay virus experimental system allowed identification of molecular determinants of viral transmission.
source: Additionally, the tractability of the C. elegans-Orsay virus experimental system allowed us to identify molecular determinants of viral transmission and will be useful for identifying additional biotic factors that influence viral transmission.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of the experimental system based on the results obtained.

claim: The C. elegans-Orsay virus experimental system will be useful for identifying additional biotic factors that influence viral transmission.
source: Additionally, the tractability of the C. elegans-Orsay virus experimental system allowed us to identify molecular determinants of viral transmission and will be useful for identifying additional biotic factors that influence viral transmission.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the experimental system.
